text.p: Europe's mobile phone major Nokia Oy said on Tuesday a strong upturn in handsets helped its first-quarter profit race ahead by over 260 percent, and this boosted its confidence for further growth and profitability.

Reporting pre-tax profit up at 1.45 billion markka ($278.7 million) from 399 million in a weak year-ago period, Nokia said its net sales climbed sharply to 11.33 billion from 7.93 billion. Earnings per share were up to 3.79 markka from 1.14.
The median analysts' forecast had been for a 1.26 billion markka profit and Nokia's stock boosted earlier gains, standing up 11 markka or over three percent to 312.00 markka soon after the report.
"It hit all the right buttons," said Neil Barton at Merrill Lynch in London: he said Nokia's revenue growth and its gross margin around 31 percent were excellent.
Nokia said its overall earnings were helped by a strong recovery in its mobile phones arm, which made a slight operating loss in the year-ago period.
Net sales of mobile phones rose nearly 60 percent to 6.15 billion markka, with telecommunications infrastructure sales advancing over 34 percent to 3.73 billion.

"Our first quarter results give us further confidence in our previously stated positive outlook for strong growth and good profitability for 1997," CEO Jorma Ollila said in a statement with the results.

He told Reuters Financial Television that Nokia had reached its target 10 percent margin in mobile phone sales in the first quarter and said handset price erosion had continued, but Nokia had "more than matched" it.
"We expect this year an average (handset price) erosion of 15-20 percent, which we can very well manage," he said.
Ollila said Nokia had "very well kept our market share" in mobile phones, "and in fact strengthened that in many parts of the world".

Barton mentioned a comparison of overall mobile handsets and systems sales growth between Nokia, Swedish rival Ericsson and Motorola. Nokia put in 48 percent, Ericsson 42 percent, Motorola four percent.
But he added since Nokia had a very weak first quarter last year, the comparison was not strictly fair.
Other analysts said investors may be cheered by the fact that Nokia had positive cashflow in the first-quarter -- at Ericsson, reporting last Friday, cashflow was in the red.
Nokia, which at end 1996 claimed the title of world number one in digital handsets, said it was "continuing to build on our position".
